Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
"Screaming Vermillian" <vermil...@yahoo.com> wrote in message
news:1105467394....@z14g2000cwz.googlegroups.com...

> Two non booster vampires in each starter AND one nonbooster library
> card. THAT'S new.

Oh my Gohd! *THAT'S* SCARY!

First of all, the non-booster vampires have been there as long as
White Wolf has been making starter decks. Sabbat War had them. And
I've been bitching about this as long White Wolf has been doing it.
They're not that far from "super rares", because you have to buy a
bunch of cards you generally won't need (after you've acquired one or
two of them, that is whole starter decks full of cards). And long-time
players have almost no need of the starters at all since they often
already own the reprints. The secondary market won't touch 'em for
the most part because it makes even less sense for them to break open
starter decks than it makes for players to buy them straight out.

This is a TERRIBLE practice and pretty much the only ongoing practice
White Wolf engages in that really steams me up!

At least in the past, it's been confined to vampires. You don't usually
need many copies of a vampire, unless it's something like Huitzilopochtli,
which lends itself to a 12-copy-of-one-vampire gadget deck.
Thankfully, I haven't noticed any starter vampires qualify for that...
so far.

But now they're doing it with library cards. Meaning that if they
should turn out to be arguably useful at all - depending on the design
of the card - could essentially become a $20+ "super rare" card. I
know that in the past, the record of extremely rare cards, promo-onlys,
and such have been pretty quote-"good"-unquote in that the cards have
fairly wall-papery or (perhaps more diplomatically put) extremely
specialized cards. I would hope that turns out to be the plan, here.
But this kind of stuff is playing with fire at best. Cripes.

> Gonna' be a bit pricey to collect this set, just like the other ones...
> and furthermore, what do we suppose the ebay prices on those starter
> only library cards will become (if they're any good of course,

Well, "if they're any good" IS the 64 million dollar question. Of
course, if they're not good, then we buy wallpaper. The path between
these two extremes is narrow and precarious, even when using design
devices such as uniqueness and "play only once per game".

But don't worry about those EBAY prices. History has shown such
cards won't be available on EBAY at all.

Fred

> Is the packaging the same? (1R3U7C) Or has it always been like this,

> just felt like commenting on it, and this following: )
>
> Two non booster vampires in each starter AND one nonbooster library
> card. THAT'S new.

There are some cards that I feel could be better off if they were
confined to the starters only. For example, I would have liked if the
Hunting Grounds were starter only. The only time they are welcome to
see as an uncommon is when you're drafting, and that is an uncommon
event in itself.

Almost any Unique card could be acceptable as starter only. Cards with
a "once per game" clause like Giant's Blood or Ancient Influence could
also work. It would save space in the larger set for the "good" cards.

Of course, if WW is intending to designate "power rares" which are
useful in multiples, such as Shroud of Absence or Alastor, as starter
only, their entire customer base will take a serious look at where they
invest their gaming dollar.

I prefer to think that WW will continue to do the right thing, but it's
a very slippery slope. One mis-step could really affect their product.
Jeff

Well, the actual answer is, when the starter is no longer avaiable.
Remember, if one card in one starter turns out to be extremely useful while
the cards in the other starters are not, then we'd have the unequal run
on starter decks - the same as the issue that comes up between the two
10th Anniversary Sets. I know we disagree about that but even if you were
right about Set 1 being deliberately overproduced, I don't think there's any
way in hell White Wolf could predict which new library card was the higher
demand one.

unnaturally useful card aside, normally the price shouldn't be more than

it just totally offends my sense of wasting cardboard, should it ever
comes to the point where people are buying whole starter decks and throwing
out all the cards but one.

Messages.Author: John Flournoy
Messages.Body:


Except that after a certain point, those commons you are getting in
your booster are completely superfluous, just like the other 87 in a
starter deck. Admittedly that number is higher than '87'...

But if you've bought a couple of boxes of a booster set and decide you
still want/need another copy of a rare, odds are that almost all of the
commons in that booster set are ones you no longer need. Nobody really
jumps up and down going 'I didn't get the Anarchs rare I wanted, but
HOORAY I got my _twenty-first_ Car Bomb!

So, yeah, initially, the boosters are a tremendous benefit, but
eventually you're just rare-fishing, and that gets prohibitively
expensive if you're hunting for one specific card.

(Plus, lots of people covet multiple cards in the starter decks instead
of a solitary rare - even if it's just more Blood Dolls.)

That said, I'm still in agreement that I hope the starter-only library
card(s) are not 'I'll take 20' but 'I'd like to own one or two and
beyond that, enh'.

> Fred

-John Flournoy

Actually I don't see a problem here. As a long-time player I don't really
need any of the reprints in a starter. So including a starter-only library
card is nice. This way I get 3 useful cards out of each starter instead of
just 2.

By the way, I expect those 4 library cards to be unique. At least I hope it
will be. After all, the new cards in the 10th anniversery set were unique as
well.

After the last few sets I think we can assume the following: White Wolf
brings out sets that are fairly easy to collect. Just look at Black Hand and
Gehenna: for almost all of the rares it is enough to own about 2 copies.
That is because the cards are unique, or they are simply not so great (like
crusades). Ok, you still need more copies if you have lots of dekcs at the
same time. But in that case you need more of all the cards out there.
Also, there are no "ultra rares" anymore like the R1 cards in Final Nights
or Bloodlines.

To be honest, sometimes I see this as a disadvantage as well. After having
opened 1.5 or 2 boxes of boosters I have practically all the cards I ever
need from the set. Right from the beginning. So it is not necessary to chase
after some elusive cards. At least for me that was part of the fun of
Bloodlines (still the best VTES set ever), not being able to build every
possible deck right after the release.

Messages.Author: Curevei
Messages.Body:
>And I've been screaming about it since Sabbat War. And I think EVERYONE
>should be bitching about it, especially estiablished players who don't
>need the other cards in the starters. I think the reason more people
>don't is that they don't quite understand how bad the problem is that
>these starter-only cards create.

It should be something I bitch about more, falling into one of my general
areas, since it's a fairness issue, to bitch a lot about. I've had to open
precons just to yank one vampire. Having 10-20 copies of the booster vampires
for a set and 2-3 of the fixed ones is kind of ridiculous since vampires are
vampires.

I guess I've let it go because I've run into so many problems with precons.
What role are they supposed to achieve for a game? Ones I've bought tended to
try to achieve multiple goals and, thus, fail to do a good job at any of them.

Starter only cards can be seen as having two purposes. For companies that want
to sell precons, they provide a reason for everyone to buy them. Begs the
question, then, why there's so much chaff in precons to go with the worthwhile
cards. For companies that don't care, they are a bonus to the customer. A
newbie could, for instance, trade them away. Except, if the card is good
enough, you essentially end up with having created the situation that precons
are meant to be sold since people will buy them just to get a couple cards.
BTW, if anyone is wondering why I'd even consider the case of a company not
wanting to sell precons, it's because it can happen that they lose money on
them, that they sell them anyway just to enable people to have a good enough
starting point for playing the game.

I don't actually have a problem with precons, though I like random starters to
exist for sealed deck play. My primary problem with the ones that get made is
how much junk they have. Why not start newbies off with a reasonable
constructed-level deck? Why not have enough good stuff to give veterans a
reason not to feel shafted when they buy them for specific cards?

Would better precons solve the "there's only 2-3 cards in here I want" problem?
Not entirely. So, getting back to what to do about vampires and whatnot, one
idea is to have the starter only vampires be 2 per precon. It's not like we
desperately need a lot of the crypt fillers we get in the precons. Crypt
duplication is common in constructed play and, if the newbie really wants more
variety, the extra copy is easily traded.

Fred, the problem is that you've confused necessity with luxury again,
and you're creating an artificial "need" in your own mind.

I have little problem finding starter-only vampires as need; all I've
ever had to do is go look for them. Show up at qualifiers and pick up
from the promo pile, buy them from Jeff, trade for them (you know,
trade?) with the guy who bought 6x starter boxes, etc...

They are available to be found. I'm sorry, Fred, I just am not going to
believe that you're out there spending ANY effort looking.

And even if I'm wrong and you're just unlucky, well, it's time to face
up to facts: If you want starter-only cards, the best route is to buy
starters. The difficulty (or lack thereof) obtaining these cards on the
secondary market is not White Wolf's concern; why are you bitching at
them about it?

Sometimes buying starters gives you more of other cards you already
have; often, you get a bunch of cards that are ALSO in the new set,
meaning you need to buy fewer boosters.

Above I mentioned an artificial need. Honestly, Fred, how many of these
vampires do you NEED to make a deck? 2, tops, right? It's rarely
effective to do more than double up on a single vampire, unless you're
running a one-star-wonder deck... and those are fairly rare, due to the
difficulty in making them work.

So once you have 2... you're set for most cases. I do not believe that
purchasing 1-2 boxes of starters is an excessive investment in something
that is purely, 100%, a fluffy luxury item that you absolutely NEVER
need to continue on with your life. I used to routinely purchase 2
boxes of starters and 2 boxes of boosters for every set; and barring
occasional booster rarity surprises, I was invariably able to make _any_
deck that I had come up with during playtest. (Gift of Bellona was a
big, ugly rarity surprise, since I typically used 6-8 in a deck during
playtest; less was just not adequate.) Starter-only cards were never a
problem for me, though.

What this comes back to is, once you have 2 copies of each vampire,
Fred, you're going to be good to go. Any artificial "need" created by
your desire to have 5-10 on hand of everything, or wishing to have
multiple decks built? That just doesn't wash. If you want to create
that artificial need for yourself, that's fine; but please don't come
crying to us about it. That's a restriction you placed on yourself, not
one that WW stuck you with.

- --
Derek

James Coupe wrote:

> commons is rarely bad. (I'm thinking, what, four starter packs here?)

Opening a starter, just to get the plumb cards and trade off the
commons/chaff to the newer players works out well for everyone. Going back
to the Assamite starter I got the other night, I got a handfull of cards I
wanted (Psyche!, Blood Doll, Legendary Vampire, Forced, a bunch of Quietus
cards I don't have enough of already, more Pursuits, whatever) and gave John
a bunch of utilitarian cards (Bum's Rush, Sport Bike, Minion Tap) that he
needed as he is a newer player. I got stuff I wanted. John got stuff he
needed. We were both pleased by the outcome.

Out of curiosity, I went and looked over some random starter decks, to see
exactly how much chaff one tended to get by picking up a starter. And
really, there isn't that much, assuming:

A) There are some good reprints you need.
B) There are new cards from the set you can use, as they are new.
C) There are some starter only cards that are hard to get otherwise.

Looking at the generally considered crappy Anarchs Gangs deck, you get:

-Eddie Gaines and Bobby Lemon, both good starter only vampires (the only 4
in the game with ANI and a group 3 one cap with pot)
-3 Blood Doll (regardless of minority opinions, these are always good)
-1 Coven (a previously rare card that is reasonably good and no one has that
many, likely)
-1 Ecstatic Agony (again, a previously rare card)
-1 My Enemy's Enemy (again, previously rare card that is actually good to
have a lot of)
-1 Force of Will (a good card that is good to have a lot of, and if you
already have too many, one of your newer groupmates can use them)
-1 Govern (the same)
-2 Wake (just like Blood Doll--you simply can't have too many in your
collection. And if you somehow do, someone else doesn't have too many)
-1 Pulled Fangs (again, previously a rare, not a bad card)
-1 Torn Signpost (everone wants these--they still go for $2.00+ each on
e-bay)
-4 Garlick's Legacy (new card for the set that you likely want a bunch of)
-3 Smash and Grab (new card from the set)
-4 Diversoion (new card from the set)
-A bunch of G3 vampires with their disciplines pushed up half an inch, so
you don't have guys with "superior silver dot" in your sleeved crypt.

And that is a crappy Anarchs deck. You get 2 starter only cards, 11 new
cards in useful numbers, 4 cards that used to be rare, and 8 very
utilitarian cards that you or someone in your group probably needs anyway.
And then a handfull of cards that may or may not be useful for you (like
Flash and Fake Out and Bum's Rush, and whatever) but will certainly be
useful to someone you play with on a regular basis. And this isn't even a
*good* Starter deck with, like, a Disarm and 2 Tastes or 2 Freak Drives and
a PTO. Yeah, ok. The CE Nosferatu starter *sucked* (and even then, I still
bought 2...), but other than that, the starter decks are pretty good, in a
value for your buck sense.

So yeah. To get starter only cards, assuming you can't manage to get them as
singles or trade for them, you need to buy a starter deck for $10.00 (well,
really, about $6.00 each if you go in on a box with some friends and order
from The Lasombra or e-bay or whatever). But unless you are *extremely*
jaded, even spending $10.00 for a starter isn't that bad of a deal, as
illustrated above.

And heck. Even if you *only* want the starter only cards and are going to
throw the rest of the cards in the trash out of spite, if you get a starter
for $6.00 (not even a remotely unreasonable expectation), you are paying
$2.00 each for your 3 "starter only" cards (assuming we are talking about
the KMW starters). Even if you were to buy them as singles and not waste
your money on a useless starter deck, would you really expect to be able to
get these cards for *less* than $2.00 each?

We'll see about buying from Jeff. He was supposed to have updated his
inventory last night and I see no BH or Anarch starter-only vampires
in his stock right at the moment. Even so, Jeff is a "public service"
dealer - I don't think he's charging the sort of premium it would require
to keep these things in stock. Therefore, to buy from him, you have to
leap on him the moment he updates. That's not the same thing as saying
"these cards are for sale".

One thing that's becoming clear: at a certain point, White Wolf printed
up a bunch of Final Nights and Sabbat War vampires and have been passing
them out in tournament packs and on their dealer tables. So if you're
tapped into one of those sources, you can obtain them. If you work at
it, quite like you can obtain handfuls of them. I guess that's good.
Even people who don't show up at tournaments can find someone who does
and eventually find them without buying starters. If they did the same
with the other starter-onlies, it would probably make a huge difference.

One of the reason I don't work that hard at finding them is that it's
just easier, in the end, to raise your hands slowly and pull your wallet
out of your breast pocket with your teeth and kick it over to the nearest
dealer of starter decks, let him loot it as he pleases, and accept the
fact that you're going to pay for a bunch of cards you don't need. That's
basically what I do to a point. But the whole thing is stupid. It
basically amounts to raising the price for the cards. White Wolf can
charge anything they want for cards and they can make certain cards as
rare as they want - which can amount to the same thing. Either way, they
can only run the scam too far before people will start complaining that
the game is too expensive.

And what I can do, other people can't necessarily do. It's easy to say,
"Just work harder and you can find this card." But if you make the chase
too hard, people eventually say, "Fuck it, I'll find another game that's
not so hard (or so expensive) to get into." Cards only cost money. I
don't know where to buy opponents.

> Honestly, Fred, how many of these vampires do you NEED to make a deck?
> 2, tops, right?

It depends on the vampire. Plenty decks have multiples of certain
vampires, even 12-vampire gadget decks. I agree, so far none of them
have been bad that way. Hopefully, some effort is being expended to
avoid it. But if they keep going on it, sooner or later I expect a
mistake will get made.

Now they're doing library cards. Again, they've done well in the past
making library cards quite specialized wherever they've needed to -
Storyline promos and the like. But I'm specifically worried that a
mistake will happen if they keep going to this well long enough.

Fred

I'm not Jeff. Nor I am I anyone who regularly sells singles on the
internet. So basically, I'm talking out of my ass, here. But anyway,
I'd figure:

A starter that sells for about $6.00 retail in bulk likely (i.e. box of
6 CE starters for $36.00 kinda deal, like Jeff and Potomac have) costs,
what, $4.00 to a retailer?

Using, like, an Anarchs starter for example, you can probably sell the
starter only vampires for $2.00 each. And at least 1 of the reprint
rares for $2.00. And probably some other specific card for a buck or
two--for instance, looking at the Gangs starter, there are two starter
only vamps (sell'em for $2.00 each. They'll sell), a My Enemy's Enemy
(a rare that people want a lot of, so it'll also likely sell for
$2.00), and a Torn Signpost (heck--there is, like, a lot of 3 of these
on e-bay right now for 8+ bucks. $2.00 isn't unreasonable to ask for a
TS). If opening a single Gangs starter results in selling those 4 cards
for $2.00 each, your $4.00 investment becomes $8.00. If you can turn
the rest of the pack into some kind of money (i.e. sell the Blood
Dolls, Deflections, and Forced Awakenings for .50 each, which also will
sell, and the rest of the deck as a parcel of .25 vampires and .05
commons that folks will pick some up of along with the $2.00 starter
only vamps), I'd think that breaking open most starters would be
modreately profitable.

I mean, yeah, the bulk of a given starter is likely to not fly off the
shelves. But starter only vampires and good rares (and every starter
has at least one of these. Well, ok, not the CE Nosferatu, but ya know,
whatever) and utility uncommons will sell quickly (assuming folks know
you have them). And if you can turn a $4.00 starter deck (as a
retailer) into $8.00+ quickly, and then squeeze bits of cash here and
there off the dregs for a while, that seems like it would be a
reasonable sales plan. But again, that is me, and I have no experience
in this sort of thing.

The problem is, however, that not all starters in a given box have that
much sellable stuff--in the Black Hand box, the !Nosferatu starter has
easily enough singles to be profitable (2 starter only vamps, Disarm,
2x Taste, all of which will sell quickly), but the other 4 each only
have, say, the 2 starter only vamps and then maybe one solid "rare"
that'll sell quickly (!Tor have Palla Grande and Art Scam; !Malk have
Deny; !Tre have Succubus and Infernal Pact?). But still, if you can get
a box of BH starters at wholesale for, say, $32.00 ($4.00 a pack), and
sell off:

-16 starer only vampires at $2.00 each ($32.00)
-2 Disarms for $3.00 each ($6.00)
-4 Tastes for $1.00 each ($4.00)
-2 Palla Grande for $2.00 each ($4.00)
-2 Art Scam for $2.00 each ($4.00)
-2 Deny for $2.00 each ($4.00)
-2 Succubus for $1.00 each ($2.00)
-2 Infernal Pact for $1.00 each ($2.00)

You end up with $58 out of a $32 investment, Not a huge profit margin,
but enough to, like, pay for the starter decks you want to buy for
yourself (assuming you are, like, The Lasombra who sells and plays).
And if you can sell off the Blood Dolls, Wakes, Deflections, Forceds
for .25-.50 each (maybe in lot sales), it isn't that difficult to
double your money.

I'm assuming here that there are some cards will *will* just sell,
based on my own experience--cards like Disarm, Taste, Palla Grande, and
Art Scam always seem to sell on e-bay, and always seem to go for more
money than I'm willing to pay (which is, like, about $2.00 per single.
Maybe $3.00 for a Disarm.) And based on the rest of the discussion
herabouts, I'd figure that starter only vampires would seel like
hotcakes for $2.00 each. But I could be wrong.

-Peter

<ira...@gmail.com> wrote in message news:1106115382.9...@z14g2000cwz.googlegroups.com...

>I know this may be crazy talk, but what if the KMW precons are good
>decks?

Well, that would be a good, helpful thing. :-)

I think I have to acknowledge a couple of points other people made
during this thread:

Curevei is right: the value of precons tend to suffer from not quite
doing anything well enough. I sympathize with the point that it's
probably not very easy choosing a set of cards that's going to turn
these babies into hot sellers for any purpose. LSJ said that they
"shouldn't be too focussed" and that's probably true. But constructed
decks need to be focussed on some level (even 'toolbox decks') or they're
lousy constructed decks.

It would be helpful if draft and sealed deck play in Jyhad weren't so
boring. Then, the 'value' you'd get with precons would be a nice
tournament that goes with them, which would make them more palatable
to buy for that purpose. But even though limited tournaments certainly
involve skill (and studying the expansion you're about to draft helps,
too), the actual tournaments are just hard to play. Everything feels like
it happens in slow motion because it's hard to mount much of an offensive,
either combat or bleed, with the number of cards you're limited to given
the price of a reasonable tournament. (That is, you can't use a precon
AND draft from 8 or 10 or 12 boosters since it would cost too much.)

The reprint choices don't always strike me as being the best ones, either.
I don't know if that's because I have different needs than the ones
imagined when the choices are made (quite likely, I suppose) or if
there's a reluctance to reprint very many old, valuable rares for fear of
upsetting too many collecters (that would be most unfortunate), or what.

One guy did mention the point that, "At least now we're getting *3*
new cards for our money, not *2*." Actually, that's pretty valid and
if I weren't paranoid about a library card turning up that becomes
too useful, I might take comfort in that point. If you want to go
that way with it, maybe there should be *more* precon-only cards -
and less rares in boosters (so older players wouldn't have to buy as
many boosters to compensate for the money spent on buying precons). And
more and better new cards from the boosters included in precons, such as
printing at least one or two new rares from the boosters in each precon.
This would definitely take the sting out of having to buy a set of precon
decks to get the precon-onlies: essentially, it adds the value that the
precons haven't had in the past.

Fred

Well, that sort of an attitude does seem screamingly circular: if no one
talks about it, White Wolf can't really be aware that there's
dissatisfaction, and hence focusses its attention in other areas.

Still, the issue to me seems mainly structural: the way the game works
and the fact that it has a large number of different ways to go about
winning it seems to make it hard to construct effective decks out of
limited resources. Or at least, out of resources limited to the practical
number of boosters and precons you can ask people to buy for a single
tournament. (I'm sure if you used 15 or 20 boosters or something, at
_some_ point you'd hit a number of boosters that would make for fun
tournaments. But not many could afford them and the time engaged in non-
game pretournament activities like drafting and deckbuilding would also
begin to get prohibitive.)

The answer that Magic tends to use (apart from just the game being
structurally more condusive to limited play) is one I hate: strewing
expansions with cards useful for limited play but not very good for
collecting and using in constructed play. You want talk about sapping
the value out of your game, try that! In fact, one of things I find
commendable about this game is that the common cards are, by and large,
useful. Not to say there aren't kind of crappy commons in the game, but
I accept these as just the difficulties inherent in designing CCG
expansions. It wouldn't make sense to chastise the designers to make
precons ultimately more valuable (MY end goal, if not others') by majorly
screwing over the value of what you can pull out of your average booster.

Other than that, I don't know what to advocate. Maybe a set of rules
for some sort of limited play that somehow allows for even better deck
construction than draft? Or maybe there's some trick(s) that the
designers could employ (or employ more often) to yield card designs that
are useful for both constructed and limited play? I can't say.

Fred

>Really, if this game is going to continue, WW is going to have to put

Why?

WW has shown a great willingness to keep older sets in print, more or
less to demand. Camarilla Edition, Sabbat War and Final Nights are all
three very good "base sets", in the sense that they have quite useful
starters and an interesting card base. (Final Nights is the weakest of
the three, but it's still usable by n00bs.)

Unlike, e.g., Magic, WW don't use the base set mechanism to cycle key
cards and strategies in and out of play. *All* cards and strategies are
available for play, subjecting to grouping.

And with a lot of expansions having starters that new players can pick
up, lots and lots of basic cards are freely available to new players.
It's not like you need a base set to make those freely available again
(as happens in games where a set goes to print once, maybe twice, and is
never seen again, so if you didn't get those cards and can't trade for
them...)

--

Like, as you mention, I think the main problem with VTES draft (keeping in
mind that I think VTES draft is very entertaining, but it is a very unweildy
and extra slow game style) is structural, and not so much the composition of
the boosters or the set or whatever.

I think that the problems with VTES draft are much deeper than simply what
cards are included in boosters and starters, and I don't think "making a
more draftable set" is really possible. That there are so many disciplines
and so many different cards and card types means that draft decks, even in
the best of situations, are going to be slow, unfocused, and difficult to
get anywhere with. But I think that this is simply how the game is
structured.

The best bossible draft situation I have ever played in (i.e. the most
condusive to making playable decks, to the the most cohesive set and highest
likelyhood of getting useable cards) was, like, 9 pack CE draft--lots of
cards, not many clans, not many disciplines. In theory, this is the best
possible situation. But still, the games were slow and gridlocky. 'Cause
that is simply how VTES draft works, 'cause that is how the game makes it
work.

Maybe if there was, like, a draft only set that consisted of, like, only 4
clans and only 6 disciplines and a very limited pool of master cards, you
might be able to pull something off. But that isn't really VTES, and isn't
really a product that has wide saleability possible.

But then, I could be wrong.

Messages.Author: Morgan Vening
Messages.Body:
On Thu, 20 Jan 2005 17:26:16 -0500, Peter D Bakija
<pd...@lightlink.com> wrote:

>Maybe if there was, like, a draft only set that consisted of, like, only 4
>clans and only 6 disciplines and a very limited pool of master cards, you
>might be able to pull something off. But that isn't really VTES, and isn't
>really a product that has wide saleability possible.
>
>But then, I could be wrong.

I don't think so. Whenever I see VTES 'draft', I just don't understand
how it works. It seems like something like 75% of cards* have some
form of restriction on them, ranging from Sect, to Discipline, to
Clan, or something even less (Titles/Anarchs/Black Hand/Seraph).

* It's less, according to ARDB, 892/1387 (64.31%), but there seems to
be an inordinate amount of crap there.

The reason why draft works in Magic, is twofold. First, you have 5
real variables for core. Which means you can reasonably pick 50% of
all possible options (two colours+colourless), and possibly a splash
of a third colour (as is common in the upper echelons of that format).

The second, is free range of 'base'. In a VTES draft, you draft your
vampires first. Each vampire has one of three sects. 1-6 of 8 common
(Ani, Aus, Cel, Dom, For, Obf, Pot, Pre), 3 uncommon (Dem, Pro, Tha),
6 rare (Chi, Nec, Obt, Qui, Ser, Vis), and 10 ultra rare (Bloodlines)
disciplines, and 1 of 34 Clans. Add to this the lesser traits, and
that's a lot of minutae. Which ups the large number of cards that will
be unusable to a fairly significant number.

Add in that this is locked in place before the regular draft comes up,
versus the Magic version of selecting your base in whatever numbers
you want, AFTER you pick your core, with very few variables to
consider. The only way I can see this transposing this to VTES, is for
there to be either a large free selection of "Take whatever you need"
vampires, or a "Construct a Clan", both AFTER the core (Library)
draft.

Personally, I don't see how VTES could really work in a draft format
in any meaningful way. The diversity, the depth of 'character', and
the strength of multiple dedicated archetypes, are what makes VTES
great. Unfortunately, they hinder non-constructed formats, in much the
same way the socio-political aspects that make VTES fun, is what acts
as a detriment to VTES 2-player. Sometimes, a square peg just won't
fit in a round hole.

Morgan Vening

Why... hmmm... lets see.

Say KMW comes out and I'm a noob. Some guys approach me about playing
this game, and so we decide to go all in together and we each buy a
starter. We check it out, are a bit confused by the rules at first, but
pull through and figure it out and start playing. We buy some packs of
KMW to expand our individual pool of cards, cause we figure: We've got
KMW starters, so lets buy some KMW boosters! What happens?

The !Gangrel and Baali guy gets a bunch of redlist and indy stuff. Same
thing with the Archon and Anathema guys, except they don't want the
occasional Baali stuff, nor do they want the occasional PRO thing. They
decide to trade, but one of the guys hates the fact that he can't find
anymore copies of Social Charm or Lost in the Crowds without buying
another Baali Precon. Some of them want Blood Dolls, but don't want
more duplicates of the rest of the stuff in the starters "What's the
point of buying another starter? I want to start playing other clans
and strategies!" Someone suggests buying a different starter, but, as a
previous MTG player, he understands that one gets more rares buying
boosters.

In comes a veteran VTES player. He's showing them great cards and game
play with Deflections, Cel Guns, Kindred Spirit bleeder, and FoS
stealer. They want to start buying boosters of set to start being able
to put together their own decks of this type!

So one of them starts to find some Final Nights. He finally finds it,
buys a bunch of boosters, and doesn't see any Temptations or Form of
Coruptions! Next month the veteran tells him that its because it was
printed in Ancient Hearts or in the FoS precon. Confused and upset, the
noob buys a FoS precon, but gets ONE of each. He is dismayed that he'll
have to buy 4-5 more of these to make the tempt deck... Another guy
wants to get into some old school Ventrue voting, so he gets some Cam
packs. He's doing well. He gets deflections and everything else.
Another guy buys into some Sabbat War and makes a Kindred Spirits deck,
with help from a Black Hand !Malk starter. Oh. Then he gets busted for
violating the grouping rule. Oh. Then other players are jealous of the
extra Wakes and Blood dolls this guy is finding in the Sabat war packs.
They're all confused and upset at dumping money and not really getting
the basic cards thye need to build multiple decks that vary a bit from
precons. "Why doesn't this game have a good base set?" they ask!

Its not that the cards aren't availible. Its that the cards are
availible in a bunch of scattered places, and each expansion doesn't
include basic needed cards, or different versions of them, so that
noobs buying these starters will have to go back to SW or starters to
find the basics.

~SV

Messages.Body:
SV wrote:
>One of these days I'd like WW to be more Noob friendly and playable
expansions...

But really, expansions *can't* be nood friendly and playable on their
own. As ever expansion comes out, the vast majority of the player base
generally expects:

-A "theme" for the set (Black Hand, Anarch, KMW, whatever)
-At least some new vampires for, like, every clan (barring, say, the
Bloodlines, that is still, what, 18 different clans or so?)
-At least one new card for every discipline (again, barring the
Bloodlines mostly)
-New cool master cards
-No reprints of stuff we already have tons of

As a result, having a noob friendly, playable new set is almost
impossible. Unless you make CE again (which isn't so much an
"expansion"). But there isn't really a *need* to make CE again, as we
have CE still. Consequently, trying to make an expansion that both:

-Covers all of the above
-Is noob friendly and playable on its own

is virtually impossible.

This being said, the expansion closest we have, really, is Bloodlines,
which is pretty self contained. But still really werid and difficult to
flesh out without having non Bloodlines vampires and cards for support.

So in reality, the structure of the game is such that expansions, by
necessity, are noob unfreindly and not really playable on their own.
But CE is both. So really, if you are looking for draft, CE is the way
to go, and anything they made that would do the same thing would be
just like CE (except filled with G5 vampires, and maybe a few cards
cycled in and out of the set). So until they do that, CE is what there
is.

-Peter

That assumes that they don't turn up in starters. Blood Doll certainly
does, for instance, and a lot of excitement has been generated by Black
Sunrise (making Wake less important). Black Sunrise may be indicative
of useful card effects being made available in different ways - you
don't need a Wake, because you can get a good Wake-like effect from this
expansion.

glancing through them, I see Computer Hacking, Threats, Skin of Rock,
KRC, Staredown, Aire of Elation etc.

obvious staple cards[0] I see with a couple of minutes work are:

8 Blood Doll (2 per starter)

4 Consanguineous Boon (!Tor)
4 Harass (!Trem)

things like Guard Dogs, bleed bounce (Telepathic Misdirection and
Deflection), bleed reduction, Bonding, Bewitching Oration, various
useful equipment (a Laptop, a Leather), and so on.

Of course, this is missing some useful stuff from your list above. But,
White Wolf happily keep older sets in print, at which point getting the
other stuff is easier.

The CE Malk starter, for instance, has 5 Spying Mission. The Nossy
starter has 3 Spying Missions, 4 Computer Hacking, 5 Bum's Rush.

don't want to buy a starter when it only has three cards I want in it"

on group three. You just happen to have some of those vampires.

Toreador you don't give tuppence for, surely?

but lots of the cards are easily (and guaranteed) available, whether or
not we have a base set.

[0] That is not to say there aren't other good cards in there - there
are. But these are generally useful cards, IMO.

My primary concern is not about Group 2--it is about the future of all
odd groupings for the Independents. If the small G3 size precedent
holds for the future, every even grouped rollout will screw the Indie
clans over again and again. Group 3 was never "complete" for the
Indies, so G4 should have never been opened up until the right time.

existence of a large Group 2 to me doesn't mean it is necessary or even
proper to severely limit the size of Group 3.

the current balance of G2/3 out of whack, nor will it hurt the future

transitional period will not happen again later down the road. Ideally,
there will be roughly the same number (12? 13?) of vampires in every
group for every sect. I just don't see why we need to wait to get this
started. The impact on G2/3 will be minimal while the benefit on G3/4
will be (and would have been) significant.

Independents when a new even group arrives.

>
> To each his own.

I guess if solving a problem just requires a solution, but perhaps not
the best one. I certainly don't think the tiny G3 is a good one at all.

> > Adding even just 2 more Indie vampires into Group 3 will *not*
throw
> > the current balance of G2/3 out of whack, nor will it hurt the
future
> > G3/4. The main thing it will do is set precedent for G5 so this

every
> > group for every sect. I just don't see why we need to wait to get
this
> > started. The impact on G2/3 will be minimal while the benefit on
G3/4
> > will be (and would have been) significant.
>
> No matter what the number of any clans vampires in any group, adding
> two more will *not* [sic] throw the then-current balance out of
> whack. You could therefore proceed, adding two at a time, to make
> any group as large as you like and defeat the grouping mechanism
> altogether.

If you made an allowance for the odd numbered groups to slightly grow,
and the even numbered groups to be slightly less, you'd eventually get
to more or less parity in group size, which I think the goal ought to
be. This makes new group roll-outs smoother for everyone involved
instead of maintaining an unearned privilege for the few that got lucky
when the Grouping Rule was introduced.

Jeff

drafting is low. In a smaller, more focused set (e.g. Sabbat War),
there are lots of vampires who can use a lot of the cards in the set.
In a watered down set, there's much less chance of getting e.g. ANI
vampires when the boosters have Animalism cards in. (See, for instance,
the difficulties of drafting Bloodlines - so much disparate stuff, so
little chance of getting what you need.)

So then you add a whole load of mechanics designed to make cards
playable - Pillar, or whatever. And in a fixed set, used only with
itself, these could possibly work.

But this ignores the fact that a set would need to be good for
constructed play as well (or else it wouldn't sell). And every time you
add cards that are generally available to other vampires, even without
the relevant disciplines, you break the design templates. Arika doesn't
have DEM, but can now play some DEM cards at Dem and/or DEM? (Alter
according to exact formulation of rule.) That's letting her do things
she wasn't designed to do and wasn't costed to do. Do you make such
cards so weak that big vampires won't need to use them? Or good enough
that they'll be an asset to such decks? It's a sticking plaster for a
draft set. It's *not* suitable for constructed play.

Then there's the fact that it breaks the general backstory. "So, why
can my Brujah use Obfuscate even though he doesn't know any?" Backstory
is not insignificant when converting players from the RPG.

A fanset does not have the real-world, commercial constraints placed on
it that actual sets have. You don't have to consider the *real* impact
of dozens of new mechanics, how to market a set ("The New Base Set!
With No Focus! And So Many Cards You'll Have To Buy Three Boxes To The
One Rare You Need!") and so on.

But you most certainly aren't addressing the needs of various different
levels of players, whether you think you are or not.

There's other ways. Cards that are only powerful in significant numbers (or
key off having some card in multitude) aren't an issue for limited play but
could be for constructed. One might make the argument that such a card would
constitute being "a more powerful card" since the criterion we use for powerful
is constructed, but it's possible to design a card that doesn't seem that
powerful until you hit some sort of critical mass. Choir would be a bad
example since it's not powerful in any amount. How about Specialization? I
consider it a powerful card, so it could fall into the "they printed a powerful
card" category, but maybe other people don't see it as that hot.

Then, there's cards or combinations of cards that are so tricky to take
advantage of but, once you find the deck for it, become extremely powerful that
will have no impact on limited play. Baltimore Purge is the sort of card that
would make sense here, but it may be too obviously good in constructed and not
bad enough for limited (I don't think I've ever seen one go off in limited, so
I have little idea). Powerbase: Berlin helps enable Turbo Arika, though it's
not like it's bad for limited play. I'm sure there's a better example out
there of a card too limited for limited and not obviously powerful in
constructed but combos into something at least kind of powerful.

I snipped the top of the post because I wasn't sure whether I was going to
comment on the differences in constructed and limited in general, but I feel
like providing an example of something. Constructed and limited are very
different games. I played in a draft earlier this month where my entire crypt
was Sabbat and I made a mistake by including The Hungry Coyote. Yet, if I had
enough vampires with the discipline, Personal Scourge would have been a
nobrainer.

Unless constructed and limited play similarly, there's always going to be
differences in the usefulness of cards. There's probably going to be
differences anyway due to the one copy versus numerous copies issue. Further,
in limited play, cards that don't see play in constructed because they are
simply inferior to other cards can be worth playing. I'll play Secret Horde or
Short Term in any realistic draft deck because I ain't got no Blood Dolls.
Does that mean these inferior cards shouldn't exist? In some cases. Drives me
nuts how Short Term keeps getting reprinted in precons/demo decks and not Blood
Doll, a card vastly more useful to the people who make the most use of these
decks.

Messages.Author: Gregory Stuart Pettigrew
Messages.Body:
> how many of those vital starter only cards were already available in
> other sets?

B5CCG had 7 precons. Four were from the (heavily errata'd) Premiere Set.
The game formula required you to have a Starter for every deck due to its
Ambassador characters, so it did get kind of annoying for heavy buyers,
but newbies rarely had to buy more than two of a given starter.

Most of the Starter-only cards from Premiere were reprinted in Deluxe,
with the "Fixed" rarity appearing once per booster pack, making them Rare
for collectors. :)

> And were any of the games generating new players who would buy the
> starters because they didn't have a collection from an out of print set?
>

B5CCG only had three out of print sets, two were from the end of the
game's run, the other was Premiere (boosters). Premiere was phased out so
that Deluxe could get the errata into play. B5CCG starters can still be
found, a couple of years after the game died.

If a newbie picked up one of the Premiere Starters during the later stages
of the game, they were pretty SOL. Most of the power cards for the main
races were scattered between the various sets, and few people were
interested in trading them.

If a newbie picked up the Psi Corps Starter, they were really SOL because
that set sold out FAST (but the starters are still widely available. I've
been buying starters just to get the Uncommons and Rares in them).

If a newbie picked up the Opposing Factions Stater, they were totally SOL
because it wasn't designed to be playable - just to provide one each of a
bunch of cards for playing two players of a given race at a time.

BUT if a newbie picked up the Non-Aligned Starter, most of the cards
they'd want were in only one or two sets.

Frankly, I have no idea how a Newbie would get into B5CCG, so I ended up
sharing my collection with my friends so that we could all use it.

The issue is really about what is the actual problem with that prevents
Jyhad limited tournaments from working well with the avaiable product
vehicles and what could you do to fix that. Proposing individual cards
willy-nilly that might not "ruin" constructed while being useful for
the limited game misses the point. And, if done en masse, could quite
easily threaten the quality of the existing constructed game. A card
that registers on the poor (moderately but not extremely useless) end
of the scale might be OK by itself. But if all the cards are kind of
crappy that way, eventaully the whole release becomes crappy.
Furthermore, if you have a specific intent that you're filling with
a given card, that might not be too bad for one instance. But if you
keep working on that same intent for card after card, eventually it will
have some kind of effect on the whole expansion which in turn will have
an effect on the game. That's why I think it's better to talk about what
you're trying to do overall before discussing specific cards or specific
mechanics on specific cards. The latter are just examples for conveying
a general idea.

Fred

>> > I don't think its possible to print a card that sucked for
>> > constructed but was great for limited.
>>
>> Clearly, you can. Of course, what sucks and what's great for limited
>> will depend on which expansions you're using in your tournament. But
>> any card that's screwed by some readily available and often used card

>> in constructed may suck in constructed but be a god card in a limited

>> environment which doesn't use its "predator".
>
> Wait. What does this mean, doesn't use its 'predator'?

Cards that make the use of other cards problematic. For instance,
Immortal Grapple causes problems to decks employing scads of Strike:
Combat Ends cards because, aside from preventing you from just waltzing
out of combat free from all those horrible things your opponent would
otherwise do to you, you wind up having to hold onto the S:CE card
and it clogs your hand. In effect, you get "punished" for playing
with a non-hand-strike. Immortal Grapple limits the use of S:CE,
preventing it from being a "god card" in constructed. (Some might
say it doesn't do enough, and that in general there aren't enough
such S:CE-limiting cards in constructed to "prey" on S:CE. That's
a separate issue, though.) Point being, S:CE might be much better
in limited than constructed since a player attempting to win with
combat strategies in limited would be highly unlikely to accumulate
enough Immortal Grapples to be useful in limited. In fact, the
reason S:CE isn't that important in limited is because combat offense
in general is so terrible that combat defense seldom matters.

The above represents the type of thinking I believe you have to do to
find solutions to the problem of printing sets that would be better
for draft. Talking about individual cards is _way_ premature until
you've thought about what you're trying to accomplish by designing
them.

(about SV's proposed mechanics)

>> In this case, I think the issue is, "Would they be too powerful for
>> constructed?" I think they would.
>
> And how would you break them? These are VAMPIRES. There are many GOOD
> vampires out there (Ian, etc...), and they haven't HURT constructed
> really, have they?

I didn't say it would break anything. They're just _better_ than
existing vampires, meaning that existing vampires would be obselesced -
which is definitely a bad thing. If you balanced such vampires with
corresponding disadvantages, then the disadvantages would likely negate
their effectiveness in limited decks as well as constructed decks -
unless you've created disadvantages that only matter in constructed or
something.

Fred

>Deal with the Devil (I as thinking the barrens, but including a unique
>probably isn't the best idea, and there's no other good hand cycler
>that I could think of that wasn't unique), 1 Generic Ally, 1 Computer
>Hack?

Generic Ally probably isn't necessary - lots of decks don't play them at
all.

I'd head for cards which are big "swing" cards. DwtD is a big swing for
draft, yes. But there are also cards like e.g. Giant's Blood which are
a potential huge boost, if you can draft them, whereas someone else get
a packet with a crappy rare instead. Of course, this depends on what
sets you're drafting from.

My experience with sealed deck and draft is that things are slow, and
not *that* interesting a lot of the time. And I'm not necessarily
terribly engaged by the deck I've got. Cards which make it more brutal
are potentially nicer for me.

For a reasonably generic start, however, I'd be tempted to include, say:

2 Blood Doll
2 Wake/Forced
2 Minion Tap
2 Deal with the Devil
2 Computer Hacking
2 Leather Jacket
1 Autarkis Persecution
1 Bribes
1 Kine Resources Contested
1 .44 Magnum
1 Melee weapon - say Bang Nakh
1 Bum's Rush
1 Harass
1 Ambush

That's along the lines I'd want to go, however - mixed enough that no
one strategy is necessarily favoured (the weapons are there for defence,
too), but varied enough that there is stuff you will probably want to
discard.

[0] That is, different staples, rather than 75 million copies of Blood
Doll. Though the starter ratios do mean they probably have several of a
lot of useful cards (3-8, say).

superior, and the 9-cap has only a Bishop title and pays 2.5 points for

Many, many cards in Jyhad are useful if you have many of them, rare,
common or uncommon.

Rare/rarer slots are often taken up by:

- unusual cards, which are a bit off the wall
- specialised cards
- cards which are likely to cause problems anyway (e.g. unique)

No-one will deny that there are some good cards in rare slots which can
be used in large amounts. What separates this from the typical Magic
situation is that you don't generally *need* to be playing that card in
large amounts to win, or to spend similarly large amounts defending
against it.

amounts. I love it, but it's not "devastating" IMO.

temporary... but I suppose White Wolf might not want to devalue existing

say:
>

defence,
> too), but varied enough that there is stuff you will probably want to

It's not a bad start. I think it's worth noting that Blood Doll and
Wake do not necessarily make *draft* better. They make your *deck*
better, yes - but if you make everyone's deck better at staying alive,
you may just be making draft games longer than they already are. It's
still probably worthwhile to put a couple Dolls and Wakes in everyone's
draft pack because it reduces the unfairness of only *one* person having
the Doll or Wake or whatever, but it's not going to make draft games go
faster, or necessarily be more exciting.

I'd really like to skip the Deals with the Devil in favor of a Dreams of
the Sphinx in every pack, but like I mentioned, I'm not sure WW would go
for it. Could be one Deal, one Dreams, I suppose, but I'm really not
convinced that Deal is a good enough card even in draft. In my
experience, hand cycling isn't all *that* crucial to draft success:
sure, I'd take The Barrens if I saw it. But the normal end-of-turn
discard is about as much hand cycling as you should need, most of the
time.

Leather Jackets, eh. I think they would make games go slower, and
favoring combat over combat defense is not a bad thing for draft games,
I think. I'd be willing to put in the two weapons even without the
Jackets. (I might go with Brass Knuckles or Gas-Powered Chainsaw over
Bang Nakh though, the lower expense makes them more worthwhile in draft
in my opinion.)

Likewise I think a KRC in every pack is reasonable, but Autarkis
Persecution should be omitted. Bribes is probably okay. Replacing the
Autarkis Persecution with a Conservative Agitation would be fine with
me. Consanguineous Boon would also be OK, though not as generally
useful. Domain Challenge or Ancilla Empowerment I would also endorse.
:-)

Three rush cards is probably more than a generic draft pack needs. One
might be enough. Certainly no need for more than two, I think.

There are, unfortunately, no generic +bleed action modifiers or stealth
cards that could really go in. (Stealth Ritus, but only if you're
playing Sabbat... ooh, Polaris Coach might be interesting.) Overall,
I'd emphasize that it's offense that draft could usually use more of,
rather than defense. The simple "keep my vampire untapped" defense is
so effective in draft that ways to break equilibrium are pretty
important, in my opinion, in making the game more exciting. Laptop
Computer might not be a bad idea... maybe.

Even an Anarch Revolt in every pack wouldn't be unwarranted, IMO - now
there's an example of a card that's not likely to look overpowered in
limited but can become annoying in numbers in constructed. :-)

Sanguine Instruction might (perhaps) be worthwhile. A couple Lucky
Blows could be nice. A couple Dodges too; that's a place that
offense/defense parity seems reasonable to me. Even a Concealed Weapon
might be cool. Fame would be cute, it'd get contested a fair amount,
but that might not be a bad thing. Hey, you know, I could get behind a
couple Life in the City rather than Giant's Blood... though the swing
effect wouldn't be real huge most of the time. Misdirection is so good
in draft that it might be worth including for the same reason as Blood
Doll, though having it generally available would make draft noticeably
more deadly I think. Sudden Reversal would be appropriate, but I don't
know if we'd like having so many Suddens in every draft game. Surprise
Influence would be funny (and is sometimes actually good in draft).

Of course, we don't really want to go over 20 cards for a draft pack...
even 20 might be rather much. 10 would probably be a better target, if
we don't want to influence the final decks to look *too* much all the
same.

Josh

Quite. Again, you're missing what the designers are trying to do
relative to what *you* would do if you were the designer. You really
need to get beyond that.

Consider: Choir is a very cool card. People want to make Choir decks
work. People need a lot of Choir to stand a good chance of making a
choir deck work. (Because, if nothing else, they need two in a given
turn or it's wasted, leaving aside the possibility of blocks.) So, what

This drives sales. The presence of cards which you need to amass in
relatively significant numbers (8-20, say) drives sales. Excluding the
presence of such cards from a set denies that possibility for driving
sales.

See, these are the sorts of decisions *real* designers make. Not just
"How can I make a set I'm happy with?" but "How can I make a set that'll
make money?" and "How can I make a set that will mean I keep my job?"

But it's not designed to be draft friendly.

You're obsessing about draft again. Unlike Magic, V:TES has never had a
strong draft scene (the wide number of disciplines makes that tricky,
for a start, which the restricted number of colours in Magic mitigates
against). V:TES has also never had a designer that's said "We make some
bad cards that are there for draft tournaments." (Also, bad cards can
force people to buy more cards, since the ones they've got are dross.
Not that Magic is a cash cow, of course.)

>
>Bad Dreams Curse

>[aus] (D) Put this card on a ready minion without aus. This minion

Cards are made rare or common or whatever based on their utility. Not
their utility to just draft. Some mistakes are made, of course, but the
design team/commonality setters have shown a strong tendency to correct
such things where major mistakes have been made. Again, not in all

>cards, I ned help making up cards that'll fit a good for draft, good
>for constructed base set).

What's significantly problematic is that you're completely fixated on
draft. Most people aren't. Draft is a fun blast now and then, but it's
not what most people care about, IME. Some, yes, of course.

However, for instance:
http://www.thelasombra.com/fanset_vermillian.txt

One with the Night
Action
pillar
1 blood
obf: This minion gets +1 stealth until the end of the turn or the end
of its next action (whichever is first). Untap this minion if this
action is successful. OBF: As above, but you may untap this vampire
even if this action is not successful.

First off, is this a good card? +1 stealth to the end of the turn, or
the end of the next action. Well, I untap once, but I need to be able
to take multiple actions for this to work out better than Lost in
Crowds, or any similar common stealth card. It's costing a blood, too!

This is a poor choice for constructed play, in many circumstances. At
inferior, if I don't have obf/for, I might as well play Lost in Crowds.
Or why not play Psychic Veil, even if I do have for? *All* my vampires
get +1 stealth that way, not just this one. Sure, it's not the same
effect, but many times, it's going to be just fine, and more flexible.

Mundane Guise
am
pillar
obf: +1 stealth on a non-cardless action. OBF: As above, but at +2
stealth. You may discard this card at the end of any succesful
cardless action.

Good for constructed? Not really, no. Again, for obf, I just want Lost
in Crowds, almost always.

Being able to discard the card also seriously undermines one of the
fundamental mechanics of the game - if I don't attempt a block, you
don't get to cycle stealth. If I don't block, you get choked. You
don't want to make cycling easy.

Also: consider the implication of pillar. Is it hard to get an action
that requires a card? No. Include Computer Hacking. Include Govern
the Unaligned. Whatever. The restrictions on, say, Shadow Body and
Shroud of Night (restricting bleeds, or votes) are much, much more
significant in this way.

And now you just hand stealth to big vampires who don't need it. The
Obfuscate vampires would rather have a good card. The vampires who
don't have Obfuscate now want to use this to get 'disciplineless'
stealth. Good design choice? Questionable, at least, which is going to
end up supporting vampires who aren't "supposed" to use it in the first
place, and be ignored by the ones who ostensibly should be using it. In
which case, you're much better off writing useful but flawed cards like,
say, Stealth Ritus, which actually address the needs of the people
concerned directly.

Scrolling down, alighting at random:

Grace of Helena
Combat
Do not replace until the next discard phase.
Prerange. Pre: Once this combat, this minion may burn one blood to
strike: end combat. Untap this vampire after strike resolution, if
this is done. PRE: As above but you may replace this card immediately.

This is actually quite well done. (You might want to clarify "if this
is done" as regards whether it's the choosing to do it, or executing the
strike, and what happens if the strike is cancelled etc.) However, at
superior, it's no better than Majesty. At inferior, it's better and
worse than Majesty. I'm unsure how much the DNR will impact in
practise, but it's a nice consideration. I might have been tempted to
go for the more vanilla "Pre: ...may burn two blood to...." and "PRE: As
pre, but burn one blood instead." Here, the cost implications are
clear, but they may well be too harsh. But I'm not sure that your
version isn't well costed.

Again, alighting at random:

Uniform Shift
Combat
pillar
pro: Strike: If the opposing minion is not choosing dodge, or combat
ends as its strike, combat ends. PRO: As above, and untap this
striking minion.

If I got this in a booster and I'm a Gangrel/Protean user, I'd be
thinking "Jesus, why the fuck did they not just reprint Earth Meld which
is simply better?" And then you've just handed S:CE to a whole bunch of
people who didn't have it, without a lot of work - again, meaning that
Protean cards don't actually support Protean.

Possibly perfectly useful for limited play, where you don't get Earth
Meld, but in constructed play when I want Protean, I'm going to take
EVERY SINGLE COPY of this card and set it on fire with little photos of
the designer stapled to it.

(I have rage issues, by the way.)

An Apple to the Victor
Reaction
1 blood
ser: Play when a methuselah is about to gain control of the edge.
Control of the edge does not change. SER: As above, but that
methuselah burns one pool.

Probably fine for limited play - you only get one, unless you're lucky.

For constructed play, I wait until my prey bleeds and then play three of
these. Generate a few SER weenies, which isn't too hard with Aabt
Kindred and some discipline cards. No, I don't make this a binding part
of my deck, for when I get a political prey, but it's a good risk in
many circles that my prey is going to bleed at some point, even in all
but the most focused political decks.

Pity the stealth and bleed deck that finds itself taking these from both
sides...

Consider: "You may only play one AAttV per action." Or: "Your minions
may only play one AAttV (in total, across all minions) per action." Or
something achieving the same effect. Or a Wake-like "Do not replace
until your untap phase" as, if played against your prey, this is going
to hurt - especially if you're using Wakes to play them. Or even: "SER:
As above, but the Methuselah burns 1 pool but does take control of the
Edge." - which leads to you not being able to play it on the *next*
bleed they take, because they already have the Edge.

You really want, need, to think "What happens if a player plays 20 of
these in a deck?" (Or more.) The original design team clearly did try,
with limits on action modifiers and so on, but they missed a number of
obvious tricks - lots of S:CE and lots of KRC being the obvious
problems. But it's an easy mistake to make.

V:TES constructed is *nothing* like limited; if a card can be put into a
deck twenty times, someone will consider it.



>

> used. Examples are good for illustrating more general ideas. :-)

I never demanded example never be used. Examples are fine to use. But
SV is ONLY posting card designs without a clue as to the overall intent,
which I'm pretty sure is bad approach, given what's at stake.

> Regardless - cards for new sets are already being designed with their
> constructed-play power taken into account. I don't think that's going
> to change. Trying to *also* consider the usefulness-for-draft of cards
> in a base set doesn't seem like a bad thing to me.

No, I don't think it's bad either - necessarily. Again, it depends on
the approach. The problem is that limited play doesn't just demand that
the odd card be sensitive to the needs of limited play. It really
requires that the entire set be geared towards using it for that purpose.
A major aspect of the problem (really THE problem, if you want to look at
it that way) is that no packs exist that will provide the numbers of cards
required to create decks with good ousting power. To fix that by just
jiggering with the design of cards means that the you'd have to keep
limited play in mind when designing large numbers of common and probably
uncommon (to a lesser extent) cards. There's no way to do this by
proposing individual cards. You have to adjust your entire philosophy of
designing cards.

>> Again, first tell me what you're trying to do. THEN propose specific
>> cards. Just creating more powerful cards clearly isn't the answer.
>
> He's trying to make cards that are usable in more draft decks than the
> kinds of cards we see now, by making them usable with either of two
> different disciplines, etc etc.
>
> Seems worthwhile to me. If the effects aren't broken in constructed,
> there's no reason they'd be problem cards.

You need to be precise about your terminology. It may not be "broken"
in the sense of allowing the creation of unbalanced decks. But if they
obsolesce existing cards in constructed, clearly that's bad. I think
these mechanics would obsolesce existing cards in constructed. The
problem with this approach is that it's just making more powerful cards
in general so they'll be more powerful in limited - but then they'll
also be more powerful than existing cards in constructed and that's bad.

> Anyway, I think you're right that there can be cards good in limited
> that aren't much good in constructed. But I don't think that's a big
> problem with making a limited-oriented base set. There are *already*
> lots of cards printed in most VTES sets that aren't very good for
> constructed. There's no reason the problem would have to get *worse* in
> a limited-oriented set.

Sure it would. It would be worse because that's your CRITERIA for
printing these cards. Ergo, they'd ALL tend towards the bad side of
the scale, making for packs that are overall a bad value for constructed
purposes.

> I don't think Vermilian's examples would obsolesce existing vampires any
> more than other new vampires do.

Then I think we just disagree about that, at least about the "Mastery"
thing. Being able to search a library for a card that one could
repeatedly use is pretty powerful. "Scout", in retrospect may not be
that good. But then, I don't think "Scout" is going to do anything
for limited.

> The 6-cap is a 6-cap with only one superior, and the 9-cap has only a
> Bishop title and pays 2.5 points for its "Fortitude Mastery" ability.

I don't care. There's just no reason these things shine in limited
but not constructed really. So they either fall in the territory of
being overpowered for constructed or not helpful for limited or some
combination of the two - point to where on the scale you think it
should be.

But if you disagree and you think they ARE better in limited than
constructed...well, why didn't we start the conversation there in
the first place? Then we can see what overall effect designing lots
of such cards will have on constructed.

Fred

Messages.Author: e...@boursorama.com
Messages.Body:
Category four, cards that are good for limited and bad for constructed
play is somewhat huge. Identifying cards in this category is a key
skill in draft play

Here are examples of this category

- Outclassed weapons : shotguns, bastard swords, bang nakhs and most
weapons are good draft cards (but completely unpalyable in
constructed). An improvised flamethrower could be a frst pick draft
card (and too dangerous a bet in constructed)

- Permanents, even suboptimal ones: Rumor Mill, club zombie, IR Googles

- "Dominated" minion cards : nimble feet (outclassed by pursuit or
psyche), media inluence (outclassed by legal manipulations), ambush
(inferior to bum's or harass) ... thet still can do the job perfectly

- anything that bloats : Short term investment being the best example

- So-so mastercards usually evicted by staple master cards (see an old
thread by Orpheus about boring staple masters, I fully subscribe to it)

- Joe-Shmoe lowcaps : any four(or less) cap without a major drawpack
can be a very good vampire. When is the last time you played Anwar in
constucted

- Some vampire with powerfull specials/titles . Guys like Lachlan,
Vasantasena, Helena or William Biltmore are ultimate killers in
limited environment (and outclassed fattie crap outside of it). William
Biltmore being the "worse" of the category, as any one who played a CE
draft tournament already knows".

were going to ramp up the power of cards in general, making old
constructed cards obsolete. Now you're saying that the draft-oriented
cards aren't going to be any good in constructed, so people who like
constructed won't buy the packs. Or are you saying that if we
*intentionally* print cards that are good in limited but not in
constructed, that worsens the existing "bad card problem"? Sure it
does, but that's not what I'm proposing. We don't *want* to make more
cards that are bad in constructed. Our goal is for all the
draft-oriented cards to *also* be good in constructed. That should work
out as well as the current (assumed) goal for all cards to be good in
constructed. (Since the current goal seems to have a significant
failure rate of weak cards already.)

any

> repeatedly use is pretty powerful. "Scout", in retrospect may not be
> that good. But then, I don't think "Scout" is going to do anything
> for limited.

Sure, Mastery is a cool ability. As I read it, though, the card is used
once and then it's gone, just as if it were played from your hand.
That's not *that* powerful. Yeah, it's kind of like Sibyl's Tongue
without the action cost, but instead it does have a blood cost, a
discipline limitation, a superior-discipline requirement, and a
hand-size/discard cost.

Scout's probably only going to do anything helpful in limited when
you're already not going to be able to afford to bring that vampire into
play. But that's at least *slightly* helpful, since you often can't
afford all your starting vampires in draft.

> > The 6-cap is a 6-cap with only one superior, and the 9-cap has only
a
> > Bishop title and pays 2.5 points for its "Fortitude Mastery"
ability.
>
> I don't care. There's just no reason these things shine in limited
> but not constructed really. So they either fall in the territory of
> being overpowered for constructed or not helpful for limited or some
> combination of the two - point to where on the scale you think it
> should be.
>
> But if you disagree and you think they ARE better in limited than
> constructed...well, why didn't we start the conversation there in
> the first place? Then we can see what overall effect designing lots
> of such cards will have on constructed.

...what? It's not necessary for the abilities to be better in limited
than constructed. They're just supposed to be helpful for limited and
not break constructed. They can be just as good in constructed as they
are in limited, that's fine. Making limited more playable doesn't have
to mean that a card or ability is useless in constructed.

Where it *should* be, IMO, is "helpful for limited, helpful for
constructed". There's no reason for an effect to have to fall into
either "overpowered for constructed" or "not helpful for limited".

Anyway. I do think Mastery is probably more useful in limited than
constructed, because vampire blood (one of the notable costs for Mastery
use) is a less-scarce resource in limited than it is in constructed -
since there's not as much ability to turn that blood into pool, it's
more likely you'll be willing to spend it on some effect, like that of
Mastery.

Scout may also be more useful in limited in that players are somewhat
more likely to build their crypts with the intention of bringing all
their vampires into play in constructed. But it's hard to say without
playtesting; it seems possible with any of these "search" effects that
overpowered combos could exist. (The Sibyl's Tongue experience leads me
to think that VTES isn't terribly prone to overpowered stuff happening
when you can search your library, but that's not an ironclad guarantee,
I suppose.)

Josh
