>> I never demanded examples never be used. Examples are fine to use.

>> But SV is ONLY posting card designs without a clue as to the overall
>> intent, which I'm pretty sure is bad approach, given what's at stake.
>
> OK. I thought the intent - to come up with ideas for making more
> draftable VTES sets - was pretty clear. Maybe he didn't say it where
> you would have seen it, though.

No, I understood that. The implication is that I think it's the
wrong approach - at least, to the extent that it involves posting
individual card suggestions in the absense of an understanding why
they should be useful to pursue. By implication, that understanding
would also explain why you wouldn't break anything in constructed at
the same time, using designs like that.

>> You need to be precise about your terminology. It may not be "broken"
>> in the sense of allowing the creation of unbalanced decks. But if
>> they obsolesce existing cards in constructed, clearly that's bad.
>
> Well, only if those existing cards are ones that aren't already
> "effectively obsolete" by not being useful now. (Even if there isn't
> currently a card that's *directly* superior to them.)

Sure. But if it wasn't clear before, I think at least Mastery would
obsolesce non-obsolete existing vampires.

>> > Anyway, I think you're right that there can be cards good in limited
>> > that aren't much good in constructed. But I don't think that's a
>> > big problem with making a limited-oriented base set. There are
>> > *already* lots of cards printed in most VTES sets that aren't very
>> > good for constructed. There's no reason the problem would have to
>> > get *worse* in a limited-oriented set.
>>
>> Sure it would. It would be worse because that's your CRITERIA for
>> printing these cards. Ergo, they'd ALL tend towards the bad side of
>> the scale, making for packs that are overall a bad value for
>> constructed purposes.
>
> ...? You were just saying that our criteria for making draft better
> were going to ramp up the power of cards in general, making old
> constructed cards obsolete. Now you're saying that the draft-oriented
> cards aren't going to be any good in constructed, so people who like
> constructed won't buy the packs.

You're getting confused because you haven't done your "thread history"
lesson. ;-) My original response was to one of SV's posts that posited
there could be no damage done to constructed by printing a set of cards
that are only equal or less powerful in constructed (that happen to make
for a good draft set). That's wrong, and the above is my proof of same.

At the same time, SV then posted a couple of mechanics for draft and
demanded I evaluate them to state what could possibly be wrong with
printing cards using them. Well, to me, one of them looks like it would
create more powerful vampires than much of what currently exists in
constructed. More importantly, neither appear to offer any mechanic that
solves problems in limited in any other way than just being more
powerful in general. This is the whole weakness of SV's approach: no
thought about how to create a mechanic that would be helpful for
the purposes of playing limited tournaments while being pretty much
neutral in a constructed environment.

> We don't *want* to make more
> cards that are bad in constructed. Our goal is for all the
> draft-oriented cards to *also* be good in constructed. That should work
> out as well as the current (assumed) goal for all cards to be good in
> constructed. (Since the current goal seems to have a significant
> failure rate of weak cards already.)

OK. I agree with that. Just, think about how to do that by design (first)
rather than by example (which should only be used to clarify what you're
getting).

>> > I don't think Vermilian's examples would obsolesce existing vampires
>> > any more than other new vampires do.
>>
>> Then I think we just disagree about that, at least about the "Mastery"
>> thing. Being able to search a library for a card that one could
>> repeatedly use is pretty powerful. "Scout", in retrospect may not be
>> that good. But then, I don't think "Scout" is going to do anything
>> for limited.
>
> Sure, Mastery is a cool ability. As I read it, though, the card is used
> once and then it's gone, just as if it were played from your hand.
> That's not *that* powerful. Yeah, it's kind of like Sibyl's Tongue
> without the action cost, but instead it does have a blood cost, a
> discipline limitation, a superior-discipline requirement, and a
> hand-size/discard cost.

But ultimately, it strikes as something that's even MORE powerful in
constructed - where you could build a deck around the power - than
limited. So how do you cost something like that? If you make it too
costly, it's actually a *bad* vampire in limited where you can't take
as much advantage of its power. If you don't, then it will obsolesce
things in constructed. This seems like a bad approach to me.

> Scout's probably only going to do anything helpful in limited when
> you're already not going to be able to afford to bring that vampire into
> play. But that's at least *slightly* helpful, since you often can't
> afford all your starting vampires in draft.

In other words, it's OK to have design a crappy vampire in limited since
the structural problems with draft already cause people to wind up with
crappy vampires in their crypt? Reasons this is an unhelpful line of
thinking left as a problem for the student to work out.

>> I don't care. There's just no reason these things shine in limited
>> but not constructed really. So they either fall in the territory of
>> being overpowered for constructed or not helpful for limited or some
>> combination of the two - point to where on the scale you think it
>> should be.
>>
>> But if you disagree and you think they ARE better in limited than
>> constructed...well, why didn't we start the conversation there in
>> the first place? Then we can see what overall effect designing lots
>> of such cards will have on constructed.
>
> ...what? It's not necessary for the abilities to be better in limited
> than constructed.

OK, sorry. Let me put it this way: There's no reason these things should
be better for limited than those cards printed in the past and still
well-balanced for constructed.

> Where it *should* be, IMO, is "helpful for limited, helpful for
> constructed".

Right. But keep in mind: cards are currently designed to be balanced
in constructed and generally turn out to be terrible in limited. So
fulfilling this goal requires a shift in philosophy somewhat (at least
for the cards designed into a limited set).

> Anyway. I do think Mastery is probably more useful in limited than
> constructed, because vampire blood (one of the notable costs for Mastery
> use) is a less-scarce resource in limited than it is in constructed -
> since there's not as much ability to turn that blood into pool, it's
> more likely you'll be willing to spend it on some effect, like that of
> Mastery.

Maybe. But I gurantee you, people will find a way to make use of a
search power that's far more valuable in constructed.

> Scout may also be more useful in limited in that players are somewhat
> more likely to build their crypts with the intention of bringing all
> their vampires into play in constructed.

Again, that just seems naive. I think you're underestimating what can
be done with a search-your-library power in constructed. One of the
reasons thinks like Magic of the Smith aren't far more useful is that
they're randomized into the library along with the things you'd use them
to search for. Put the power into the crypt, and I think it would be
very valuable - certainly more valuable than in limited where you're
restricted to the best card you drafted. In the case of these powers,
you're restricted to the best thing you drafted of a certain set of
limitations (which in constructed you could make sure matched up right).
If you happen to have drafted the limited "god card" (something like
Enchanted Marionette) and a Scout or Mastery vampire that finds it, then
you have a "god deck" and the tournament will become horribly unbalanced.
If you aren't so fortunate, I don't think these powers mean that much.

Fred

<jtdu...@yahoo.com> writes:

>"James Coupe" <ja...@zephyr.org.uk> wrote in message

>> In message <1106583698....@z14g2000cwz.googlegroups.com>,
>> Screaming Vermillian <vermil...@yahoo.com> writes:
>
>> >Starters are nuetral for draft. Printing staple cards ONLY in
>starters,
>> >or rather not printing/making enough in any quantity in the boosters
>to
>> >make them draftable, is bad for draft.
>>
>> And bad for established players if you print crap-loads of them.
>>
>> Lots of established players don't want to hack through base sets
>getting
>> more Saturday Night Specials. They want to get the cool new cards.
>
>Too late! Camarilla Edition *has* Saturday Night Special in it.

I know, and there were many whines from established players at the time
at the lack of cool new cards, forcing them to buy a crap-load of
boosters.

The wider issue there, however, was card ratios in Camarilla Edition,
IMO.

>Any base set is probably going to have stuff that established players
>don't want in it. It's the nature of a base set. Staples ought to go
>in the boosters of a base set because it *is* a base set. There can be
>other cards to attract established players, and there certainly should
>be. But staples shouldn't go *only* in the starters. (And they don't.
>Though Saturday Night Special wouldn't be my example of a good staple.
>:-)

No, I'm not saying they should only go in starters. (Obviously, they
*could*.) Anarchs has a number of reprints in the boosters for the
Gangrel, for instance. But filling up boosters with cards established
people don't want won't help with sales, either.

But the cry of "Won't somebody think of the newbies?" is fundamentally
flawed. They can already get a lot of staples from starters, and these
are very, very helpful for newbies. I *know* that I can get workable
cards that will give me a useful deck right now.

As I become an established player, I might want to get more, yes -
perhaps so I can have four or five decks built at once, or so I can
build a specialised "lots of masters" deck with a crap load of Blood
Dolls for my Embraces, or something.

But as a newbie, people being able to say "Well, buy those two decks and
pay mix and match, you've got a bunch of useful cards in them, and
they're both a bit combatty, so you'll probably enjoy them if you liked
the fighting in that demo deck" is significantly more useful than "Well,
buy a bunch of boosters and you might get some cards you like."

Saturday Night Special isn't bad, but it's generally not good. It was
more of an example of "This is the sort of thing that turns up in base
sets that established players will not want to collect more of." If
you're happy with Jackie Therman or IR Goggles as a maneuver away
defence, IMO Saturday Night Special isn't too bad. Where it falls down,
IMO, is that for that extra pool, .44 Magnum is better - cheap defence
in Jackie, cheap defence with offence in a Magnum, so SNS is somewhere
in between the two and a little unsatisfactory as a result.

>> If the base set boosters are just giving them more staples (which they
>> already have) or very similar staples (e.g. giving them Forced
>Awakening
>> instead of WwEF), they're not getting much new.
>
>It might not all be that new, but it should be useful. They're going to
>buy boosters because they don't want more of the exact same thing that
>was in the precon, and because buying boosters is what CCG players do.

Oh, sure. But there's no actual need to buy the base set ones because:

>If the base set boosters have enough interesting and good cards in them,

they'll be happy enough with them anyway, 9 times out of 10.

>> If the boosters are giving them cool new stuff, they could just go and
>> buy any set with cool new stuff. They already have the staples - even
>> you agree that they have many of the staples[0] now. So they don't
>need
>> to buy base set boosters to give them more.
>
>Some sets are more useful than others to people with small collections,
>though. Cool new stuff is relative.

Hard to say. Anarchs is possibly poor, but mostly because Anarchs is
hard to get working and there's quite a lot of it in there. The
fallback mechanism and hot, hot, hot vampires (in some cases) in
Bloodlines means it isn't necessarily a bad choice - the cross-over
isn't too bad. I like a lot of the Black Hand set, though a lot of it
doesn't focus too much on the Black Hand with a lot of more general fun
(or Sabbat) too. Gehenna has some good stuff, and some of the events
can be a worthwhile inclusion in a number of decks.

There's a lot of good vampires about in many of the sets, too.

<suggestions for a fixed draft set>

>I'm not sure Deal with the Devil is good even in limited play. As
>Vermillian said, it is one of the few non-unique hand cyclers. Dreams
>of the Sphinx might be nice, since even though it's unique, it's
>temporary... but I suppose White Wolf might not want to devalue existing
>Dreamses quite *that* much, heh.

A fixed include in Final Nights, Precon Giovanni. So it's available for
however many shiny pennies you can get one of them for. It's not a bad
starter, either.

>I wouldn't put Giant's Blood in a fixed draft pack either; its "once per
>game" nature makes it as dubious for everyone to automatically have one
>as a unique master.

No, the bigger problem is that if you happen to get a strong card like
that, it can give a deck a big boost. In constructed, it's no real
issue since you can build a deck around as many or as few as you want.

One of the significant problems with draft/sealed deck, IMO, is the
ability for cards like that to turn up and give someone access to
something that you have no hope of accessing.

A more vague problem with limited formats in general is that, for
example, a typical political deck will probably want a good few vote
pushing cards. But between, say, Bewitching Oration and Bribes, you're
likely to get a very small number in any draft - and much more unlikely
to get Cryptic Rider or Awe. Whereas you're much more likely to get a
lot of political action cards, with no way of passing them. Ditto, when
that card comes out, you're unlikely to have a Delaying Tactics to
counter it - so a LOT of common considerations are completely screwed.

Also combat: you need to get blocked, or have a Bum's Rush (or similar).
But again, the amount of combat cards you get is likely to be high,
whilst in a set with all of Bum's Rush, Harass, Ambush and Haven
Uncovered, you're unlikely to get a usable number.

In general: V:TES has several strategies which benefit greatly from
'gateway' cards. The obvious one that doesn't is S&B. If you get a
bleed action, you can play it just as though you were bleeding for 1.
If you get a stealth modifier, you can play it too. If you get a bleed
modifier, you can play that too. Or any subset of the three.

Hence a lot of limited formats seem to heavily favour trying to make
your deck into a (bad) stealth and bleed deck.

>It's not a bad start. I think it's worth noting that Blood Doll and
>Wake do not necessarily make *draft* better. They make your *deck*
>better, yes - but if you make everyone's deck better at staying alive,
>you may just be making draft games longer than they already are.

True, but a lot of the game has built up assuming that you'll get a
reasonable blood flow off vampires with Dolls and Taps and the like.

I would be hard pushed to believe that any White Wolf created card, for
instance, that has a significant pool cost hasn't had LSJ or Steve Wieck
or whoever is involved with suggesting/writing/costing cards thinking:

"Well, they're going to put this in their deck playing Minion Tap,
aren't they?"

(Where Minion Tap is actually any one of a number of pool generation
cards - Consanguineous Boon, say, or Tribute to the Master. Alter
according to taste.)

IMO, it would be bad (read: lacking variety) for a set to not have that
sort of range of cards - from the free Trifle that has a minor effect,
through the 2 pool tasty location, the 3 pool clan toy up to the 5 pool
ally from Hell. And the top end of these sort of cards drive the need
for pool gain, since you can't otherwise afford them without taking a
major action hit by having a lot less vampires.

This can be filed under: why making a set useful for limited is much
harder when you also want the set to be useful for constructed, too.

However, IMO, they make draft "better" for the reason you note below -
they make it fairer:

>It's
>still probably worthwhile to put a couple Dolls and Wakes in everyone's
>draft pack because it reduces the unfairness of only *one* person having
>the Doll or Wake or whatever, but it's not going to make draft games go
>faster, or necessarily be more exciting.

>I'd really like to skip the Deals with the Devil in favor of a Dreams of
>the Sphinx in every pack, but like I mentioned, I'm not sure WW would go
>for it.

A card like Dreams would be cool - but it suffers from the unique
problem already highlighted. Ditto, The Barrens and Fragment.

A card like Visit from the Capuchin might be okay, since it's so short-
term. Dreams isn't so bad from that point of view either, but you can
deliberately hold on to Dreams to annoy others whereas it's much harder
to do that with Visit.

I'm not necessarily suggesting Visit explicitly, but a limited cycler
like that might be possible.

>Leather Jackets, eh. I think they would make games go slower, and
>favoring combat over combat defense is not a bad thing for draft games,
>I think. I'd be willing to put in the two weapons even without the
>Jackets. (I might go with Brass Knuckles or Gas-Powered Chainsaw over
>Bang Nakh though, the lower expense makes them more worthwhile in draft
>in my opinion.)

I was looking at Brass Knuckles, but I couldn't decide on a low level
weapon I actually liked. Gas Powered might be a good option, though - I
was mostly looking at Knuckles, Cleaver, Poker, Bastard Sword and
similar.

However, I didn't feel the Leather Jackets would be too problematic, as
they're one-shot and the set includes several "Get into combat" cards,
plus any you draft.

>Likewise I think a KRC in every pack is reasonable, but Autarkis
>Persecution should be omitted. Bribes is probably okay. Replacing the
>Autarkis Persecution with a Conservative Agitation would be fine with
>me. Consanguineous Boon would also be OK, though not as generally
>useful. Domain Challenge or Ancilla Empowerment I would also endorse.
>:-)

Autarkis Persecution was for a different sort of pool gain, as above.

>Three rush cards is probably more than a generic draft pack needs. One
>might be enough. Certainly no need for more than two, I think.

I find the high volume of combat cards relative to the low availability
of "get into combat" to be a problem. You can't actually hit back
against your predator. And if you're acting, you can't easily Wake
(since you don't have many) to block him, and so on.

I'd be reluctant to drop down to one, certainly.

>There are, unfortunately, no generic +bleed action modifiers or stealth
>cards that could really go in. (Stealth Ritus, but only if you're
>playing Sabbat... ooh, Polaris Coach might be interesting.)

I'd rather you had to pull stealth, to be honest.

>Overall,
>I'd emphasize that it's offense that draft could usually use more of,
>rather than defense. The simple "keep my vampire untapped" defense is
>so effective in draft that ways to break equilibrium are pretty
>important, in my opinion, in making the game more exciting. Laptop
>Computer might not be a bad idea... maybe.

I was thinking of that, but as a permanent bleed modifier it's quite
dependent on how early you draw it. That's true of any of the
permanents, obviously, but.... It just feels icky.

>Even an Anarch Revolt in every pack wouldn't be unwarranted, IMO

UG SMASH

SMASH

SMASH JOSH SMASH

>Sanguine Instruction might (perhaps) be worthwhile.

Interesting, given my thoughts about discipline cards.

> A couple Lucky
>Blows could be nice.

I'm not sure - I was trying to provide cards that wouldn't be useful in
EVERY deck, but which could be of use to a wide range of decks. That
is, if a draft pack is created that means that players include ALL of
the cards, it's failed.

>A couple Dodges too; that's a place that
>offense/defense parity seems reasonable to me.

I'm not really sure that the difference between Dodge and Leather Jacket
is. (You know what I mean, I hope.) It's not like you're going to be
up against dozens of Immortal Grapples making Dodge a poor choice
though, I guess.

>Even a Concealed Weapon
>might be cool.

Concealed Weapon struck me as poor - if you don't have many equipment in
the first place, including one on the off chance you get both in your
hand at once seems poor.

>Fame would be cute, it'd get contested a fair amount,
>but that might not be a bad thing. Hey, you know, I could get behind a
>couple Life in the City rather than Giant's Blood...

My thoughts on Giant's Blood were rather more "If this is available for
drafting, it's a swing card so..." If it isn't available in the sets
you're drafting from, it doesn't matter. (Parity Shift is similar, but
the requirement means I'm less inclined to care.)

Life in the City and Lucky Blow move me more towards "would be put in
all decks" rather than "would be considered and put in some decks" than
I'm comfortable with.

>though the swing
>effect wouldn't be real huge most of the time. Misdirection is so good
>in draft that it might be worth including for the same reason as Blood
>Doll, though having it generally available would make draft noticeably
>more deadly I think. Sudden Reversal would be appropriate, but I don't
>know if we'd like having so many Suddens in every draft game. Surprise
>Influence would be funny (and is sometimes actually good in draft).

Misdirection - your earlier comments about leaving people untapped to
block jar with this, a little. If you don't have the wakes available,
Misdirection is a top card - sufficiently so that I wouldn't want to see
it draftable, really.

>Of course, we don't really want to go over 20 cards for a draft pack...
>even 20 might be rather much. 10 would probably be a better target, if
>we don't want to influence the final decks to look *too* much all the
>same.

Agreed. My suggestions were aimed more at useful but questionable to
achieve a similar end.

>> > Constructed. (short term, secret horde). But do these cards truly

>>

>> Yes, they would. If _any_ of the cards in the set were arguably

>> useful for constructed (a condition that's effectively impossible to
>> avoid), then people wanting to use them would have to buy packs of
>> cards containing mostly bad cards to get a few good cards. That's
>> bad. In general, creating whole expansions of cards that are bad for
>> constructed is bad - because they create expensive rares.
>
> Yeah, but aren't we already in that situation? There's TONS of cards in
> gehenna that are crap, but I'm chasing some of them that aren't (mostly
> the vampires! :P). So I keep buying packs and I keep loading up on
> stunt cycles, Diamond Thunderbolts, Black Hand Ritual and so forth.
> Hell, I even get crap rares too! (Crusades and some events).

No, sorry, my impression of Gehenna is not the same. Of course, some
people always seem to have the impression that any given set doesn't
contain enough cards that are powerful enough to be worth collecting.
(Sometimes different people depending on the set, too.) I think I
always encounter a bit of frustration myself with the number of cards
in many of the expansions that don't seem to be as effective as they
should be for the cost. Whether that's a flaw in the design of the
various sets or just my lack of ability to use the cards effectively
is something I can't say.

In any event, it's a separate issue. If you think Gehenna is generally
unworth collecting, then I'd say that a set of cards designed to be
good in limited but bad in constructed would be even worse in this
respect.

> Is it so bad if these bad cards were actually somewhat better for
> limited?

If they're "somewhat better for limited" then by logic they must be
relatively worse for constructed. (Worse, even, than what you
encountered in Gehenna.) This makes the constructed-useful cards
that _are_ in the set relatively much more expensive to collect.
Yes, it is "so bad".

> And the way you're talking about it, you seem to think that ALL the
> cards in a limited friendly set would be bad for constructed. Not true.

Not "all" as in every single one of them, no. But if this is the
philosophy you pursue in order to design a set of cards specifically
for limited, a preponderance of them - or at least a significantly large
percentage of them - would have to be. This triggers the problem.
Or say it triggers the problem to the extent you use this philosophy
of design. The point is to answer your original question up at the
top (remember that?!?): "Aha! Finally, cards that are truly Good For

Limited Not So Good for Constructed. (short term, secret horde). But do
these cards truly HURT the constructed environment anymore than just
reguar ole' bad cards being printed?"

The answer is, "Yes. They do." The designers do not set out to create
"bad cards" on purpose.

Fred

Yea, but not deliberately congregated in a single set. Again, my point
is that you have to consider all the implications of where your design
philosophy is leading you.

> If all crap cards were somehow converted into bad for constructed

> whatever for limited into just as bad for constructed and good for
> limited, then we'd have a like super increase in sets' draft friendly
> natures.

Sure. But that's not doable. Bad cards don't exist (or at least I would
certainly HOPE not) because some designer somewhere said, "Heehee, this
card is REALLY GONNA SUCK!!!" They don't design bad cards on purpose.
They most likely design bad cards because it's just very difficult to
design 150+ good cards every expansion. Some just don't turn out right
when they're let loose on the whole community of players using the
entire set of available cards to build decks. You can argue that other
designers might do a better job, but I'm pretty sure given the available
time and resources a designers has, there will always be _some_ bad cards
no matter who's doing it.

So you've got to assume however you change your philosophy of design,
count on the new philosophy being executed well in some cases and poorly
in others. You can't just change the philosophy in some magic way the
culls out all the "bad cards" and replaces them with "bad-in-constructed-
OK-in-limited" cards.

Fred

playing with a deck I don't actually care for? In a Magic draft in a
local store, I can get most of this done in a few hours. Yeah, the huge
tournaments for money or whatever draw a lot of people. But there you
can be doing all sorts of crap in between games - trading, eating,
walking around stalls, whatever. Much harder to do when the game you're
playing takes up two hours, and you want to fit two + a final (or three

One aspect of dial-a-crypt (the problem that grouping attempts to solve)
is creating perfect crypts. You don't *need* perfect crypts is every
reasonably sized vampire can do everything.

blood or you get +1 stealth. One with the Night - already discussed.
Mundane Guise - another +1 stealth. In the Shade - hands out -1
intercept. Body of Worms - another -1 intercept. That's a bit more

Actually, I've seen it turn up in a potentially very strong deck - the
Anarch Revolt deck with weenies. Includes enough Presence to demolish
you, and defend itself, and outvote you when you come after it.
Typically uses Elder Kindred Network.

However, you're missing a significant point here. It's hard to get
people to call votes, if they don't want to. If you have a political
deck on the table, it's a crap shoot as to whether it's your prey (or
predator) or not.

Bleeding is a fundamental facet of the game. Garfield intended it to be
so, by making it cardless and making it responsible for the Edge.
(Which is useful for political decks, as well as its pool gain uses.)
Bleed happens a lot.

Also, you're missing how easy it is to get Ser weenies - Aabt Kindred
aren't the greatest vamps but they don't contest.

>> Pity the stealth and bleed deck that finds itself taking these from
>both
>> sides...
>
>So what! Punish the stealth bleed mechanism a bit! The meta is allowed
>to change.

Sure, but why hit stealth and bleed? It's a pretty balanced mechanism
these days.

Picking a random mechanism and trying to weaken it for no particular
reason is a bit shit.

>> V:TES constructed is *nothing* like limited; if a card can be put
>into a
>> deck twenty times, someone will consider it.
>

You're not realising what that means in practise, though.

>I'm going to change the pillar rule perhaps... Maybe "if you control a

>alliance with others... but then are these suddenly useful in limited?
>Or did I just KILL their utility all to hell... Probably the latter.
>
>I think I prefer my old method of making those cards. Three levels on
>each card. Outferior, playable by ANY, inferior and superior as
>(slightly less powerful) normal...

In either case, the increased cyclability means you want to tone the
power of the cards down - which then means there's an issue of why the
discipline heavy constructed decks wants to include them.

Or you have a card which is equally powerful to Lost in Crowds, so the
Obfuscate deck considers it, but significantly more cyclable - so
obsolescing Lost in Crowds.

The Bloodlines disciplines cope better with this, as their disciplines
are far harder to access in the first place and were released with
fallback levels as a designed in facet. So the ones without a fallback
level fit in unique facets and/or are more powerful than might otherwise
have been allowed, but don't compete amongst themselves.
